pi.name: Anthony Vecchiarelli
pi.title: Associate Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology and Associate Professor of Biophysics
pi.bio: Anthony Vecchiarelli earned his HBSc and PhD in Molecular Genetics and Microbiology at the University of Toronto with Barbara Funnell. He completed postdoctoral training at the National Institutes of Health with Kiyoshi Mizuuchi as a Nancy Nossal Postdoctoral Fellow. At the University of Michigan his laboratory uses genetics, cell biology, biochemistry, and bioinformatics to understand how bacteria spatially organize fundamental processes in the cell.

lab_description: The Vecchiarelli Lab studies how bacterial cells organize their organelles and other components at the subcellular level, challenging the outdated view of bacteria as disorganized sacks of molecules. Rather than cytoskeletons and motor proteins, bacteria use ParA/MinD-family ATPases to position protein-based organelles. A central model is the carboxysome, the Rubisco-containing compartment responsible for almost half of global CO2 fixation, whose positioning by the McdA/McdB system the lab has characterized. The lab also asks whether bacteria form membraneless biomolecular condensates that compartmentalize biochemistry, and how multiple ParA/MinD ATPases coordinate the trafficking of disparate cargos in the same cell, using organisms such as Synechococcus elongatus and Halothiobacillus neapolitanus. The group combines genetics, cell biology, biochemistry, quantitative microscopy, and bioinformatics.

research_areas.title: Organelle trafficking and homeostasis
research_areas.summary: Spatial regulation of bacterial organelles, especially carboxysomes, which contain Rubisco and are responsible for almost half of global CO2 fixation. The lab investigates how cells position these organelles via the McdA/McdB system.

research_areas.title: Material state of bacterial organelles
research_areas.summary: Whether bacteria form membraneless compartments (biomolecular condensates) like those found in eukaryotic cells, and whether such phase-separated structures compartmentalize biochemical reactions.

research_areas.title: Coordinated organelle trafficking
research_areas.summary: How multiple ParA/MinD ATPases coordinate the positioning of diverse cellular components in a single cell, using Halothiobacillus neapolitanus, which encodes seven such ATPases, to understand how trafficking is synchronized with the cell cycle.

news.text: Postdoc Y Hoang was invited to the Rising Stars Symposium at the University of Chicago Department of Microbiology and received the MCDB Postdoctoral Research Award.
Jordan Byrne won the MCDB Service Award and Claudia Mak earned the Biological Chemistry Graduate Research Award.
Joe Basalla's paper on McdB phase separation was published in eLife with an accompanying eLife Digest.
Jordan Byrne began a CBTP Fellowship internship with ONL Therapeutics; Jordan and Claire passed their Checkpoint #2 evaluations.
Anthony Vecchiarelli delivered the Farrand Lecture; Claudia gave an oral presentation and Joe a poster at the ASBMB conference.

joining: The lab welcomes applicants with interests in biochemistry, microscopy, or quantitative biology. Postdoctoral candidates should contact Dr. Vecchiarelli directly with a cover letter describing their background, a CV, and reference contacts. Graduate students join through rotations after admission to MCDB or PIBS. Freshman and sophomore undergraduates may apply through UROP; juniors and seniors can email Dr. Vecchiarelli directly.
